title: Reforj
description: An open world sandbox developed at 4J Studios
overview: At 4J Studios I worked on engine and UI features across our internal tools and game projects. My main focus was integrating the Noesis rendering backend with our in‑house rendering engine, making sure the pipeline behaved consistently and played nicely with the rest of the tech. I also built several in‑game UI scenes using Noesis, working with view‑models and XAML to support designer‑driven workflows. Outside of UI, I implemented post‑processing effects such as bloom, vignette, and depth of field. A big part of my time was spent on internal tools for artists and designers. This included various small editors and utilities, but most notably the in‑house texture editor, which I helped extend and maintain as it became a core part of the content pipeline. Overall, my role was about contributing practical, reliable features to the engine and tools team, and helping improve the workflows used across the studio.

title: Isosurface Algorithms (DX12)
description: Marching Cubes, Surface Nets and Dual Contouring implemented on the GPU

media.alt: A poster showcasing the marching cubes implementation.

overview: My honour thesis explored three isosurface algorithms: Marching Cubes, Surface Nets, and Dual Contouring. The primary goal was to implement these algorithms on the GPU and evaluate their performance and visual quality. I developed a real-time terrain editor to visualize and interact with the implemented algorithms.

content.title: Marching Cubes

media.alt: A wireframe render of marching cubes terrain.

content.description: Marching Cubes was implemented in a compute shader using . The algorithm evaluates a uniform cubic grid of scalar points, checking each cell corner against an isovalue to determine which parts of the cell are within or outside of the isosurface. An integer is generated, based on the number of active corners, which is used to look-up a table of pre-configured edges representing the layout of the triangles.

content.title: Dual Contouring

media.alt: A wireframe render of surface nets terrain.

content.description: The second isosurface algorithm I explored was the Dual-Contouring algorithm. Unlike the Marching Cubes algorithm, Dual Contouring generates precisely one vertex per cell and considers the sign change along the edge of the cell. A sign change is indicative that the isosurface passed through that edge. The Surface Nets algorithm places a vertex in the center of a cell, whereas Dual Contouring uses an quadratic error function to determine the best position to place the vertex. Both dual-algorithms generates clean geometry and are better suited at preserving sharp features.

title: Foundation Engine
description: An on going personal project exploring game engine development

media.alt: An image of the foundation engine editor.

overview: Foundation Engine is an ongoing personal project where I explore game engine development. The main focus of the project is to explore and research how systems are architected and the intercommunications between these systems.

content.title: Graphics
content.description: The foundation engine has seen a couple of rendering back-ends, from OpenGL 4.6 to DirectX 12. Currently, the rendering interface is implemented through NVRHI, Nvidia's abstracted rendering interface.

content.title: ENTT
content.description: Integrated into the world context (also referred to as the 'scene'), ENTT serves as the engine's main entity component system (ECS), enforcing a component based architecture. The world context owns and manages the entity registry, where entities are made accessible. Foundation also supports scriptable entities, allowing for custom behaviours and logic.

content.title: Services Registry
content.description: A debated topic in the game engine communicated, a services registry is implemented adhering to the service locator pattern, supporting global access to engine subsystems, like the file manager. An instance of the services registry is created in the core application and injected into each layer of the application. Long term, I'm aiming to refactor the service locator, and instead manage and expose subsystems within relevant contexts. For instance, the world context will own the AI Subsystem, which wil be made available to all scriptable entities. This approach should avoid global access and highlight dependencies.

title: Graphics Programming (DX11)
description: Showcasing several graphics programming techniques in shaders

media.alt: A screenshot of the DX11 scene rendering several graphics techniques.

content.title: Vertex Manipulation
content.description: The application renders a standard plane whose vertices are displaced in the vertex shader using a height map. It also supports swapping in a grid of tessellated patches, showcasing dynamic tessellation as well as vertex displacement performed in the domain shader.

content.title: Dynamic Tessellation
content.description: A GPU‑accelerated LOD surface‑patch system was implemented using the hull and domain shaders. Each patch was defined by a 12‑point control mesh uploaded from the CPU, and tessellation levels were dynamically adjusted based on the camera’s position. This allowed high‑detail vertex displacement close to the viewer while reducing geometric complexity at a distance.

content.title: Gaussian Bloom
content.description: The post‑processing system uses Gaussian and box blur techniques. After the scene is first rendered to a target, a mask is generated from that render and stored in a secondary texture, which is then used during the blur pass.

content.title: Shadow Mapping (PCF)
content.description: Shadow mapping was implemented for both directional lights and spotlights, supporting hard and soft shadows. Soft shadows use PCF filtering, with configurable kernel sizes of 3×3, 5×5, and 7×7.

content.title: Normal Mapping
content.description: The application supports normal mapping by reconstructing world‑space normals from texture‑space data using the TBN matrix (tangent, bitangent, and normal). In addition, a per‑vertex and per‑pixel normal generation method was implemented using partial derivatives. This allows normals to be computed on the fly, adding significant detail to lower‑resolution height maps.

title: Procedural Generation (DX11)
description: An application showcasing several procedural generation techniques implemented on the CPU and GPU

media.alt: A screenshot of the DX11 scene rendering a height map and procedural waves.

overview: In the procedural methods module I implemented several procedural techniques on the CPU. The following techniques were implemented in a DX11 framework: Hydraulic Erosion, Trochoidial Waves, Voronoi Noise (GPU), Simplex Noise, Perlin Noise, Improved Perlin Noise, Octave Perlin Noise, Ridged Perlin Noise

content.title: Perlin Noise
content.description: Perlin noise forms the foundation of most procedural techniques in this project. The Perlin algorithm was implemented in C++, using the original C version as a reference. The improved Perlin variant and the Simplex noise algorithm were also implemented, and either can be used to drive the terrain generator.

content.title: Hydraulic Erosion
content.description: The Hydraulic erosion algorithm implemented aims to simulate the erosive features exerted on terrain from water droplets. Water droplets erode the terrain through bilinear interpolation across four vertices taking into account the gradient at each point. If the droplet identifies the current cell is a pit, the droplet releases sediment until the pit has been filled.

content.title: Trochoidial Waves
content.description: Trochoidal waves were implemented in the vertex shader and textured using a Voronoi noise pattern. The algorithm models wave motion by displacing vertices with sine and cosine functions. To produce sharp troughs, each vertex is offset relative to its original position—its anchor point—in both the x and z directions, creating circular motion. Wave amplitude is controlled using the ratio s / k, where s ranges from 0 to 1 and k is defined as 2𝜋 divided by the wavelength.

content.title: Voronoi Noise (GPU)
content.description: Voronoi noise was implemented on the GPU to generate cellular patterns used for texturing and surface variation. The algorithm computes the distance from each fragment to a set of feature points, producing the characteristic cell structure of Voronoi diagrams. This GPU‑based approach keeps the implementation lightweight while still providing visually distinct patterns that can be used to enhance terrain and wave effects.

title: Animation Systems (C++)
description: A project exploring animation systems and techniques in 2D and 3D
overview: In the Animation Systems module, I implemented a range of core systems and techniques, including an Entity‑Component System, a 3D blend‑tree animation framework, a 2D armature JSON parser, a 2D skeletal animator, a sprite JSON parser, and a sprite animation system.

content.title: 2D Sprite Animation
content.description: An armature parser was implemented to read and extract skeletal animation data from a JSON file. The parser loads all information required for 2D skeletal animation—such as bones, skin data, and frame information—and stores it into components for use by the animation system.

content.title: 3D Animation
content.description: A 3D skeletal animation system was implemented with support for keyframe interpolation and animation blending. The system integrates with an entity‑component architecture, providing flexible and modular control over animation data. A blend‑tree system was also developed to enable smooth transitions between animation states based on user‑defined parameters.

content.title: Blend Tree
content.description: A blend tree system was implemented to let users build complex animation behaviours with minimal code. The tree supports several node types, including Animation Clip, Linear Blend, 2D Blend, Additive Blend, Ragdoll, and Output. It also handles multiple data attributes, allowing fine‑grained control over different aspects of each animation.

title: Up For Delivery
description: A 3D puzzle game developed in Unreal Engine 4
overview: In the summer of 2022, I worked as part of a team to develop a 3D puzzle game in Unreal Engine 4. The game, Up For Delivery (UFD), is a single-player experience where the player must navigate through a series of increasingly difficult levels by solving puzzles and overcoming obstacles. My main contributions to the project included level design, scripting gameplay mechanics using Blueprints, and implementing materials.

content.title: Project Management
content.description: Utilized project management tools such as Jira to facilitate effective communication and task tracking within the team. This ensured that all team members were aligned on project goals and deadlines.

content.title: Materials and Scripting
content.description: Implemented various materials to enhance the visual appeal of the game environment. Additionally, scripted gameplay mechanics using Unreal Engine's Blueprint system to create interactive elements and ensure a cohesive gaming experience.

title: Networking
description: A networking project developed during my studies
overview: During my studies, I undertook a networking project where I developed a multiplayer networking system for a game. The system was designed to handle real-time communication between clients and the server, ensuring smooth gameplay experiences even under varying network conditions.

content.title: Boids Algorithm
content.description: A boids based flocking system was implemented to simulate the collective behavior of autonomous agents. The algorithm incorporates three primary rules: separation, alignment, and cohesion, allowing the agents to navigate the environment while avoiding collisions and maintaining group dynamics.

content.title: Prediction and Interpolation
content.description: To ensure smooth and responsive movement of networked entities, prediction and interpolation techniques were employed. Prediction allows clients to estimate the future position of entities based on their current state, while interpolation smooths out the movement by calculating intermediate positions between received updates.

content.title: Testing and Optimization
content.description: Using tools to simulate various network conditions, the networking system was rigorously tested to identify and address latency, packet loss, and jitter issues. Optimization strategies were implemented to enhance performance and ensure a seamless multiplayer experience.

title: Neural Networks (Unity)
description: A project exploring the use of neural networks to train agents to complete a simple race track.
overview: The goal of the project was to train agents to navigate a simple race track successfully. Each agent is rewarded for travelling the greatest distance from its spawn point and receives additional bonuses for reaching checkpoints without crashing. Every agent is driven by a neural network composed of multiple layers of weights. These weights are initially randomised, and with each new generation, the most successful agents pass their networks forward. To introduce variation and mimic real‑world behaviour, each generation undergoes a small amount of mutation, slightly altering the agents’ weights.
